posts.text: I think I can say, at least for me, why Claude's writing is so freaking awful, even when it's completely correct. After a big story like the Microsoft outage and FAA outage make headlines and garner a lot of attention, the media seems more likely to report on smaller outages that it may have otherwise overlooked, because it's now a hot topic. For example, 2 years ago direct deposit was broken for CapitalOne. Their customers didn't get their paychecks for several days. What would normally get deposited early on Wednesday (for a Friday payday) didn't actually hit accounts until something like Tuesday of the following week. I don't recall seeing anything in the media, all I saw were people on Twitter tagging CapitalOne support left and right, talking about how they couldn't feed their families... and I only saw that because I went looking for it. posts.title: Tell HN: HN is being scraped for emails to scam
posts.text: I know that many folks here post their personal emails in the Who's for Hire monthly pages and other places, and want to remind you that this public site gets views from folks with ill intent (or their bots/agents) as well. I use unique emails for every site, so I immediately knew that the late AWS payments email sent to my HN email were fake. There were other tells, but I want to remind everyone to be vigilant! HN is public but even social media sites where you supposedly can make your page private I've had some of those emails suddenly have spam sent to as well. Please be safe everyone! My favorite tells that an email is a scam: - Before opening a surprising/suspicious email, hover over the sender name to see the domain the sender came from (don't open the email if it's strange). - _If_ you already opened the email, before clicking any links in the email, hover over them to see the domain that the link sends you to. There are dozens more tips but a full article would be required, and these two will prevent you from falling for nearly all of them.

The signal-to-noise ratio has increased greatly since then. I've received two spam emails and one legitimate email so far, which is a huge improvement.

comments.text: A suite of high-dopamine games which use smart exercise bikes as the control interface. When playing Zwift, Rouvy, etc, I find that I get too competitive and ruin longer workouts by trying to keep up with or sprint past people who are much faster than me over long distances. This is bad for building stamina and endurance, but I get bored, and it's hard to fight boredom and physical strain both at once. I do not get bored sitting in front of Balatro, Raccoin, Tetris - anything with bright colours and satisfying noises and combos. The first finished prototype game is very simple: you sort coloured marbles. Higher watt output from the bike means marbles are blown, by wind, upwards as they roll across the screen. Lower watt output means they fall. Steady watt output means they move horizontally. Marble goes into correct hole -> satisfying noise. It rewards steady watt output over time, with minor adjustments, which is what I'm trying to work on right now. I was pretty amazed by how engaging I found it (total iPad baby brain). The miles really fly by - I get tired before I get bored. I think that next I'll either do a tower defence game, or a less-dopamine-rewarding game in the style of Kerbal Space Program. Taking your actual weight and watt output, putting a bike with wings into a physics engine, and the gameplay loop being unlocking increasingly large airplane pieces, and designing - then flying - increasingly ridiculous airborne bicycles seems like a compelling idea, though less good for fitness. The control surface being so limited - essentially one measurement which can either go up or down - is a really fun constraint for creativity.

comments.text: I worked at a sports company forever ago, and ever since then, I've wanted to build my own NBA scores + stats site. After a few false starts over the years, I have a new concept called Center Court that I'm so excited about. It's primary purpose is for live boxscores because all of the major sports sites have terrible UI/UX experiences. I always defaulted to ESPN.com but it's so slow and awful. Center Court is basically a bridge between espn.com (or nba.com) and more advanced stat focused sites that don't offer a good live experience. The technical implementation behind it is quite novel in this space too. Instead of storing computed statistics in a database, I store raw play by play payloads immutability and everything else is derived from those and can be trivially rebuilt so the event log is a derived cache of the payloads. Every stat on every page is a pure fold over the event log at request time; no derived number is stored. This enables some powerful features like being able to re-derive a game's entire state at any point of the game (or even a time range). Example game to try out: https://centercourtlive.com/game/0022600197 The site is meant to be extremely fast. It's all server-side rendered with progressive JS enhancements. URLs are immutable and cached behind a CDN. https://centercourtlive.com/

posts.title: Ask HN: Do you still enjoy coding in C++?
posts.text: In the recent years C++ received a lot of backlash due to its complexity and (perceived) feature creep. However, since C++11 I really enjoyed writing C++ with its strict type system (including const), range-based for loops, smart pointers, and how much you can do with templates. On the other hand, I know that it can be very tricky to write, for instance, a correct iterator, to get handling of rvalue references right, or to read error messages that involve templates. So, do you enjoy or dislike writing C++ source code and why?

comments.text: Oh, C++. C++ feels like an old lover who I think fondly of. We were together many years, until about C++20, through thick and thin. It was exhilarating - blazingly fast, perhaps irresponsibly so, but heck, the ride was wild. It taught me so many things, and shaped me into the programmer I am today. But we went our separate ways when its shortcomings became too large to bear, and its behavior - too often undefined - no longer excusable. I keep up with it because I still have love for it, but I have to admit I am deeply concerned about many of the life choices it is making. I should have seen how problematic it was, because I knew its history, but I had hope that it could change, and it just looks like it never will. I'm still rooting for C++, even though I am very happy with my new primary language, Rust. I hope it changes to the better, because I really want the best for it, but right now I'm just not seeing it. It keeps repeating old mistakes (e.g., more UB footguns with every new feature), without addressing any of the big flaws (insufficient tools for building robust software). I sometimes still write C++, but I'm not excited about it the way I used to be. When I do write C++, it's because I have to. When given the choice, Rust is simply just a better choice for almost everything I do. Right now, I don't see a future for C++ and me.
comments.author: simonask

comments.text: I'm really torn about C++. I love C++ but there are things that I really don't like about it as well. It's a fantastic language in a lot of ways, but it carries around 40+ years of cruft, of things that you wouldn't do like that if you were inventing a programming language today. I haven't written C++ professionally for many years at this point, and my memories of using it professionally (pre C++ 11) are not happy ones: having to agree on a strict subset of the language that we were allowed to use, which avoided features that any of the compilers didn't support well, or that my teammates didn't like. Sadly back then the list of forbidden features included templates and namespaces. But using C++ on personal projects nowadays, and being able to choose which bits of the language to use - and which to avoid - is much more enjoyable. And honestly, the language did get a lot better from C++ 11 onwards.
comments.author: chris_j

comments.text: In one word: Power. C++ is by far the most powerful language around. And this is for the best and (often) also the worst. In term of generic programming, control on hardware, capacity of abstraction and more generally expressivity: Nothing, even today, come even close to C++. It is a language full of foot guns and it has its fair share of legacy problems. But if you learn to avoid it (throught experience and pain). You can reach a productivity and a level of performance in C++ which is very difficult to beat with anything else, including Rust. Ironically, I find it particularly true in the age of A.I. Because the amount of C++ around is so tremendous, that agents are currently pretty good at it if guided properly.

comments.text: I enjoy writing C++ code. I acknowledge that C++ is a bad language in a lot of ways, but it's a bad language which I know really well, and it fits with how I think about code. And it lets me effortlessly do "clever" things with how memory is managed to avoid unnecessary allocations etc. I've already learned most of its idiosyncrasies, handling rvalue references/move semantics, how to go about implementing contracts like iterators and containers, etc. I also like writing Rust, and I like how Rust makes sure I don't make mistakes. I think Rust is a better language in many ways and I think it's the future of low-level programming (and I think it's wild that it took so many decades to get a proper competitor to C++!). But I also like how C++ doesn't care and lets me do whatever I want without acting as a nanny. I would never ever dare to write a publicly exposed web server in C++, but a game? Sure!

I still appreciate its many merits but since a bit more than a year I migrated to Rust and I find it very difficult to look back, except for maintaining my previous C++ projects. Surprisingly, it's not Rust's memory safety features that I miss the most when turning back to C++. It's mostly the absence of algebraic data types and pattern matching, and the split between compile-time and runtime polymorphism, i.e. concepts vs virtual classes, where in Rust you just have traits and use them for everything. On top of that the tooling and the ecosystem are just amazing. There's a proposal for pattern matching sitting there under the committee's desk for some years now. With the mess that the standard committee is going through I really doubt they will be able to ship pattern matching for C++29 or even later. Too little too late. So to answer the question, yes, I still appreciate the merits of C++ but I don't enjoy writing it as much as I have in the past.

posts.title: Ask HN: How did you convince family and friends to join your XMPP/Matrix server?
posts.text: I love open-source software and open protocols, but my family and friends primarily communicate through SMS for exactly the reasons in https://xkcd.com/2365/ Whenever XMPP or Matrix threads pop up on HN, several commenters casually mention their "friends and family XMPP (or Matrix) server." How did you convince friends and family to move away from SMS/WhatsApp and replace it with a niche messaging app? My family and friends aren't hardcore nerdy, but they're more tech-savvy than average. Their needs in messaging are mainly pragmatic: they want ease of use, reliability, and fun features. They don't care that much about privacy, decentralization, or extensibility (though I care about those things a lot). I've been experimenting with self-hosting XMPP and Matrix servers and clients in the past week, and the UX is even worse than I expected. It seems like all the clients either imitate Slack, imitate Discord, or imitate hot garbage. I haven't seen any that try to be a simple, friendly replacement for SMS. I'm a software developer who uses computers all day, and I find the UX for most of the clients incredibly hard to use. The only angle I could see to pitch XMPP/Matrix to people for non-philosophical reasons are that there's a more consistent experience across iOS/Android. The biggest shortcoming I think is visible to regular users is that there's feature degradation and missing information when iOS users have SMS conversations with Android users, especially in group chats. For people who have successfully won family and friends to XMPP or Matrix, what was your pitch? What do you recommend others do to make XMPP or Matrix an attractive experience for a regular person?

comments.text: I know this isn't the answer you want, but I sell people on Signal based on the user features. I’ve had great success in getting my friends and family to adopt it. Signal is incredible user friendly, privacy respecting, the gold standard for encryption, cross platform, etc. Yes, it’s centralized, yes it’s imperfect in many ways, but it’s easy and it’s pretty damn good. If you want to help the people around you to become more involved in understanding and owning their tech, it has to be an easy and good experience. It has to be tangibly better, not just abstractly better with tangible downsides. I use XMPP, but would never try to convince my friends and family to use it; it’s too complicated, the user facing apps all suck (Snikket and Cheogram are the best of the bad lot), and the incentives to use it aren't there. As you said, it’s just not attractive to a regular user, since it’s all around a worse experience than what they currently use. The one exception is that I do occasionally recommend XMPP for SIP access via jmp.chat to some of my more technical friends who have a tolerance for clunky user experiences in favor of privacy and affordability. I am holding onto an unreasonable hope that Signal or Whatsapp or others will consider XMPP+OMEO in the future to popularize the standard, but that is extremely unlikely. Matrix also is an unfortunately terrible alternative to discord (even Element is a rather lacking user experience), so while I have pushed to move groups there before, I no longer recommend Matrix. I suggest signal or nextcloud as alternatives when possible; the remaining large groups who need the closed server forum style system are usually unlikely to move to Matrix anyway.

comments.text: My advice is not specific to Matrix but other self hosted private services. Some of this may or may not be feasible with Matrix. (I have never used Matrix) - Whether family or friends, always suggest it as a "fallback" for when "preferred service" is down and to use when discussion ultra-sensitive topics or sharing financial files. With time they may just stay connected to it if the friction to do so is low. It has to be their choice, not yours. - What helps? Add more incentives such as perks that "preferred service" does not offer. No file size limits. No or few file type limits. No content filters. Add emoji's or gifs that align with their inside jokes and their style of humor. Keeping random people away is very important. Making your friends and family administrators or moderators and let them decide how it operates. Do not moderate or power-trip over your friends or family or they will leave. Limit rules to "Do not break the laws of this country in public chatrooms" and private chat rooms if you do not physically host the server . Database and file backups become even more important but they will feel in control of a thing. Have a keyword or code word they all learn means to go check the private platform that "primary platform" would not recognize. Maybe when they see "Turtle Farts!" they know to go log into your service. - They may just stay on their primary preferred service. Every group is different and not every group will see the benefits of your fallback service. They may not appreciate the work you put into setting it up for them. Do not expect to get the friends of your friends and family to move to your service. They may not appreciate the OpSec value until "Bad Things"(c)™2038 happen to enough people. Just be there for when it does. - If there are concerns that you would spy on them, consider instead using eJapperd or Prosody as you can implement OMEMO for individual and group end-to-end encrypted messages. Set up TLS fingerprint checks from multiple locations to reduce the risk of MitM attacks until XEP-0474: SASL SCRAM Downgrade Protection is fully supported and active by default on both servers and all clients. This is the only thing holding me back from setting up a public Prosody server as 0474 is still experimental. See [1] - Avoid (block) federation on private servers for friends and family otherwise it is not a private server. [1] - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=37955264

I also try to make sure my server has useful bots, a small thing but every bit of utility and differentiation with proprietary services helps. I share guides on how to get back in, one thing people get confused about is that they don't have to give PII but they do need to remember the home server URL and save their key and password. So making sure to have ready pointers and blurbs on how to login that you can share quickly is necessary because people inevitably get logged out, especially iPhone users get confused easily (for app store culture reasons I think) and need kind but eager assistance. I try to make sure we have well moderated safe space e2ee rooms to talk about hard issues, and people do realize over time that certain things are more awkward to say digitally if you know it could be being surveilled or tracked, even the metadata. I've also encouraged technical friends to run their own servers and federate, got a couple to actually do it which is a cool feeling. It takes time (years), patience, and effort, but many little pushes will build a community.

comments.text: I'd rank them like this - this comes from applying LLM's since GPT-3 autocomplete API, teaching people how to use them, giving talks to developers, answering their questions, training my own models and seeing how people interact with them: 1. Building your own model - this will cost you a bit, but is without a doubt the best way to earn concrete AI skills. From picking the data to training, seeing how it evolves, improves and scales. You will understand the "hyperplanes" of a model's inner world better than anything else can teach you. You will learn how to pick data, how it impacts model quality, way of thinking, scores, personality. If training your own is too much, start with a completed pretrain and toy with it. 2. Building a harness around a completion model - I'd put this as second best to understand the inner worlds of LLM's. It helps you build intuition around how prompting really works, how they form the answers, how to build around that. Then you can do an SFT for your own harness. 3. Building a harness and an orchestrator around finished models - this takes the bronze. It teaches you how harnesses, agents and swarms actually work, how they shape the model's thoughts and actions, how models interact with them, how they can be applied and how they can work without humans. .

comments.text: Nowadays the arrival of frontier LLMs has opened new scenarios. Agentic AI can be used to get things done, and this is important: we ourselves become architects and build by ourselves the tools we need. But there is a use that few people make: using LLMs as patient teachers that we can ask to explain things that at school, or at work, we never understood. For example I always had problems understanding the Linux graphics stack, yet over time LLMs explained to me well how everything works. I also used agentic AI to develop personal projects, work that in other times would have required the involvement of an entire team of developers. We have in front of us a wonderful scenario, but also a dangerous one: learning and working together with AI systems, or losing control of our lives.

comments.text: I personally would say: Learn how to think like an engineer. As in: - Be able to analyze a situation into processes and discrete steps - Be able to describe the actual (!) problem you want to be solved - Be able to describe how to verify that the problem is actually solved - Be able to ask the right questions regarding HOW the problem has been solved in order to gain understanding and to identify the next steps and improvements - Be able to identify when the AI gets stuck or down a rabbit hole and to guide it out of there. - Understand what LLMs are good at and what they are not good at. And there are tons of things they are not good at. Disclaimer: This is absoluty not based on any scientific study or so :-) Just my personal experience! Feel free to disagree. But my experience comes directly from my work: I have a lot of customers on my platform that are not engineers, but make use of AI to solve business problems through automations. Nearly everytime when they are stuck (or burning through a sh*tload of tokens in no time), it is because one of those skills aren't present. So I try to teach them more and more how to "think like an engineer". And often when it lands, they become much better at using AI in a very short time. The best learners are often those that already had some kind of engineering background. Now granted, the frontier models can help themselves pretty well and often can produce amazing results with very bad input. But they are also expensive. If you work with less-than-frontier, those skill requirements become very salient again. And thats what we do. We mostly work with models like Deepseek flash or GLM Flash or even local ones like Qwen3.7 .

comments.text: Watch the 3Blue1Brown YouTube series on machine learning. Understand how these things work and that they are not magical all-knowing answer machines or even anything intelligent - they are next-most-likely-word predictors. That's all. Demistify and keep that in mind with everything you do afterwards. I presume you don't want to drop thousands of dollars on video cards so pay Sam/Dario your 20 bucks a month. Ask the LLM to build things you have already done before. You need to know the correct answer so you can evaluate the solution the LLM provides you. Start with single-file scripts you have written, you can do this in just the ChatGPT or Claude web interface. Start with a vague prompt which doesn't specify many constraints or details. See what they get right and wrong. Try being much more specific and detailed. Make it ask you questions about what you want before it starts work. Try the small/old/dumb model with no thinking and try the big/new/smart model with full thinking and notice the difference in capability. Learn to setup an agent software in a sandbox of some kind. I prefer Pi in a Podman container, with only access to the project directory, but there are a million options out there these days. From this agent software, ask for explanations on a codebase you already know. Again the purpose is to know the answer in advance so you can evaluate the response provided. Ask it to just tell you some answers. Ask it to give you a code flow and reference to read more yourself. Build something larger, like a program across multiple files. Again try being vague and being specific, see the difference in what it spits out. Use it to troubleshoot a problem you have solved, like your favourite bug, and also just a boring regular bug. Try different types of issue. Learn to create an AGENTS.md for a project or SKILL.md for reusable instructions anywhere, but don't stuff it full of useless nonsense you think the model needs. Build it from experience of only what the thing gets wrong. Some people say you can ask LLMs to write their own md files, but imo these things generate way too much text. You could ask it to do that as a starting point then trim it down to remove all the extra unnecessary verbose crap. Through all this, try asking it the same thing multiple times in different new sessions. Notice the answers vary. Sometimes it gets it wrong and sometimes right. Same question, same model, same everything, different answer. Notice you need to know the right answer to evaluate the response. In situations where you don't know the answer yourself, hopefully you've seen enough wrong answers now to not trust it. Use these things to guide your own investigation, like the exercise above where you asked for code flow and references to read yourself. I think of this as "LLM as search engine, not answer engine". That seems to be 95% of what people use these things for. This set of skills would have been useful for the last 18 months and seems to be the way the industry momentum is moving at the moment.
